clinicalPearls: Chronic pain persists beyond normal tissue healing, commonly defined as lasting more than about three months, and often becomes a condition in its own right rather than a symptom
It is best understood through a biopsychosocial model, since biological, psychological, and social factors all influence the pain experience and disability
Assessment should characterise the pain (nociceptive, neuropathic, or mixed and nociplastic), functional impact, mood, sleep, and the patient's goals
Management is multidisciplinary and multimodal, combining physical rehabilitation, psychological therapies such as cognitive behavioural approaches, and carefully selected medications
Neuropathic pain often responds better to agents such as certain antidepressants and anticonvulsants than to conventional analgesics
Interventional options, including nerve blocks, radiofrequency procedures, and neuromodulation, may help selected patients within a broader plan

Long-term opioid therapy has limited benefit for most chronic non-cancer pain and carries risks of tolerance, dependence, hyperalgesia, and harm, so it requires careful selection, review, and often deprescribing
Realistic goals emphasising improved function and quality of life, rather than complete pain elimination, guide effective long-term care
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic pain involves persistent changes in the peripheral and central nervous systems. Ongoing nociceptor activity and inflammation can sensitise peripheral nerves, while repeated input drives central sensitisation with amplified spinal and cortical responses, reduced descending inhibition, and reorganisation of pain-processing networks. Neuropathic pain follows damage or disease of the somatosensory system, producing ectopic firing and maladaptive plasticity. In nociplastic pain, altered central processing generates pain without clear tissue damage. Psychological and social factors modulate these pathways, and this neuroplasticity explains why chronic pain often persists independently of the original injury.
additionalDifferentials: Progressive or undiagnosed structural disease (e.g. malignancy)
Neuropathic pain from a specific nerve lesion
Fibromyalgia and other nociplastic pain conditions
Depression and anxiety contributing to pain and disability
additionalInvestigations: Comprehensive biopsychosocial assessment including function, mood, and sleep
Validated pain and disability questionnaires to track outcomes
Targeted imaging or nerve conduction studies only when a specific treatable cause is suspected
Screening for depression, anxiety, and substance use
Medication review including opioid risk assessment
redFlags: New or changing pain with features suggesting malignancy, infection, or fracture
Progressive neurological deficit or signs of cord or cauda equina compression
Systemic features such as weight loss, fever, or night pain
Signs of opioid misuse, escalating use, or overdose risk
reference.prognosis: Chronic pain is frequently a long-term condition; while cure is often not achievable, multidisciplinary management can substantially improve function, mood, and quality of life, whereas reliance on escalating opioids tends to worsen outcomes.
pitfalls: Managing chronic pain with escalating opioids despite limited benefit and rising harm
Neglecting psychological and social contributors within a biomedical-only approach
Failing to identify neuropathic pain that needs different medication
Missing red-flag features that indicate serious underlying pathology
Setting unrealistic goals of complete pain elimination rather than improved function
management: Multimodal, biopsychosocial management coordinated through a multidisciplinary pain service and centred on function and patient goals
Physical rehabilitation with graded exercise and activity pacing as a foundation of treatment
Psychological therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy and acceptance-based approaches
Rational pharmacotherapy, using antidepressants and anticonvulsants for neuropathic pain rather than relying on conventional analgesics
Cautious, risk-assessed use of opioids with avoidance of dose escalation given its association with worse outcomes
Interventional options including nerve blocks, radiofrequency procedures and neuromodulation for selected patients
Treatment of comorbid depression, anxiety and sleep disturbance, with support for self-management
